mainEntity.name: How many data types does Java have?

acceptedAnswer.text: Java has two categories of data types. Primitive types: exactly 8 — byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, and boolean. Non-primitive (reference) types: unlimited — String, arrays, classes, interfaces, enums, and any class you define. The 8 primitive types have fixed sizes regardless of platform, which is a key part of Java's Write Once Run Anywhere guarantee.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between primitive and non-primitive data types in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Primitive types store the actual value directly in memory (stack). They have a fixed size, cannot be null, and have no methods. Non-primitive (reference) types store a memory address (reference) pointing to the object on the heap. They can be null, can have methods, and their size is not fixed. All non-primitive types ultimately extend java.lang.Object.

mainEntity.name: What is the default value of each primitive data type in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Default values for instance/static variables: byte=0, short=0, int=0, long=0L, float=0.0f, double=0.0d, char='\u0000' (null character), boolean=false. Important: local variables do NOT get default values — you must initialize them before use or the compiler gives an error.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between float and double in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: float is 32-bit (4 bytes) single-precision — accurate to about 7 decimal digits. Requires 'f' or 'F' suffix: 3.14f. double is 64-bit (8 bytes) double-precision — accurate to about 15-16 decimal digits. Decimal literals like 3.14 are double by default in Java. Prefer double for most calculations; use float only when memory is critically constrained.

mainEntity.name: What are wrapper classes in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Wrapper classes are object representations of the 8 primitive types: Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Float, Double, Character, Boolean. They are needed when an object is required (collections like ArrayList only hold objects, not primitives). Java automatically converts between primitives and wrappers via autoboxing (primitive to wrapper) and unboxing (wrapper to primitive).

articleHeader.title: Java Data Types — Primitive & Non-Primitive
articleHeader.subtitle: A complete beginner's guide to all Java data types — 8 primitive types, non-primitive reference types, sizes, ranges, default values, literals, wrapper classes, autoboxing, and type casting with working code examples.

blocks.text: In the previous chapter, we learned about Java Blocks — code blocks, static blocks, instance blocks, and scope rules. Now we cover one of the most foundational topics in Java: Data Types.

Every variable in Java has a data type — it tells the compiler two things: what kind of value the variable can hold, and how much memory to allocate. Java is a statically typed language, which means you must declare the data type of every variable at compile time. This is what makes Java programs reliable, predictable, and fast.

items.text: Both categories of Java data types, all 8 primitive types in depth, non-primitive reference types, Java literals, wrapper classes, autoboxing/unboxing, type casting, and how to choose the right type for your use case.

sections.title: Two Categories of Java Data Types

blocks.text: Java data types fall into exactly two categories. Understanding the fundamental difference between them is the first step to mastering Java memory management and object-oriented programming.

rows: Unlimited — all classes, interfaces, arrays, enums
byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean
String, int[], Scanner, ArrayList, your own classes
A memory address (reference) pointing to the object
Reference on stack; object data on heap
Not fixed — depends on object structure
Yes — all reference types extend java.lang.Object

blocks.label: Primitive vs Reference — Memory Concept
lines: // PRIMITIVE — value stored directly in the variable
int age = 21;          // 'age' holds the value 21 directly
// NON-PRIMITIVE — variable holds a reference (memory address)
String name = "Rahul"; // 'name' holds the address of the String object
// the actual characters 'R','a','h','u','l' are on the heap
// null means the reference variable points to nothing
String city = null;    // city holds no address — not pointing to any object

blocks.text: Java has exactly 8 primitive data types. Their sizes are fixed by the Java specification — unlike C/C++ where sizes can vary by platform. This platform independence is a key part of Java's Write Once, Run Anywhere guarantee.

items.title: 4 Integer Types
items.text: byte, short, int, long — for whole numbers. int is the default choice. Use long for very large numbers. Use byte/short only when memory is critically limited.

items.title: 2 Floating-Point Types
items.text: float, double — for decimal numbers. double is the default choice (and the default for decimal literals). Use float only when memory is tightly constrained.

items.title: 1 Character Type
items.text: char — stores a single Unicode character using 16-bit UTF-16 encoding. Can also store any integer from 0 to 65,535 representing a Unicode code point.

items.title: 1 Boolean Type
items.text: boolean — stores only true or false. Used for conditions, flags, and logical decisions. Cannot be cast to/from numeric types (unlike C/C++).

sections.title: Integer Types — byte, short, int, long

blocks.text: Java has four integer types for storing whole numbers (no decimal part). They differ only in size and therefore the range of values they can hold. int is the most commonly used integer type.
byte — 1 Byte
byte is the smallest integer type — 1 byte (8 bits). Range: -128 to 127. Used when memory saving is critical — in large arrays, file/network I/O streams, or image pixel data.

blocks.label: byte Examples
lines: byte pixelValue = 64;      // grayscale pixel — 0 to 127 range
byte fileFlag  = 0x0A;     // hexadecimal literal — value is 10

blocks.text: short — 2 Bytes
short is 2 bytes (16 bits). Range: -32,768 to 32,767. Rarely used in modern Java — int is preferred unless you are working with binary protocols, audio samples, or legacy systems.

blocks.label: short Examples
lines: short year     =  2026;     // fits comfortably in a short
short audioSample = 15000;  // raw PCM audio sample

blocks.text: int — 4 Bytes (Default Integer Type)

int is 4 bytes (32 bits). Range: -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647 (about ±2.1 billion). This is the default integer type in Java — integer literals like 42 are int by default. Use int for counting, indexing, loop variables, and general arithmetic.

blocks.label: int Examples
lines: int population = 1400000000;   // India population — fits in int
// Numeric literals with underscore (Java 7+) — for readability
int cardNumber  = 1234_5678_9012_3456;  // not valid — too large for int

blocks.text: long — 8 Bytes

long is 8 bytes (64 bits). Range: -9.2 × 10¹⁸ to 9.2 × 10¹⁸. Use long when your value exceeds the int range — world population, millisecond timestamps, file sizes in bytes, database IDs. Must add L or l suffix to long literals (uppercase L preferred — lowercase l looks like 1).

blocks.label: long Examples
lines: long epochMs          = 1_700_000_000_000L; // Unix timestamp in ms
// Missing L suffix — compile error if value > Integer.MAX_VALUE
// long big = 8100000000;   ← ERROR: integer number too large
long big = 8_100_000_000L;  // ✅ correct with L suffix

blocks.text: Java has two floating-point types for storing decimal numbers. Both follow the IEEE 754 standard. The key difference is precision and memory size.
float — 4 Bytes, Single Precision

float is 4 bytes (32 bits) — single-precision IEEE 754. Accurate to approximately 7 significant decimal digits. Must add f or F suffix to float literals — otherwise the compiler treats them as double.

blocks.label: float Examples
lines: // float x = 3.14;   ← ERROR: possible lossy conversion from double to float

blocks.text: double — 8 Bytes, Double Precision (Default)

double is 8 bytes (64 bits) — double-precision IEEE 754. Accurate to approximately 15–16 significant decimal digits. Decimal literals like 3.14 are double by default. Prefer double for all general decimal calculations.

blocks.label: double Examples
lines: double distance = 384400.0;            // moon distance in km

items.html: ⚠️ Floating-point precision warning: Neither float nor double can represent all decimal values exactly — this is a property of IEEE 754 binary representation. Example: 0.1 + 0.2 does not equal exactly 0.3 in Java (or any language using IEEE 754). For exact decimal arithmetic (money, banking), use java.math.BigDecimal.

rows: General decimal math — always prefer this

blocks.text: char is a 2-byte (16-bit) unsigned integer that stores a single character using UTF-16 Unicode encoding. Range: 0 to 65,535 (Unicode code points \u0000 to \uFFFF). Unlike C/C++ where char is 1 byte (ASCII only), Java's char supports the full Unicode character set.

blocks.label: char Examples
lines: // Character literals — enclosed in SINGLE quotes
// char can be treated as an unsigned integer
System.out.println(ch + 1);      // 66 — arithmetic on char returns int
System.out.println((char)(ch + 1)); // B — cast back to char
System.out.print(c + " ");  // A B C D E

blocks.text: boolean stores only two values: true or false. It is used for conditions, flags, control-flow decisions, and any binary state. The actual memory size is JVM-dependent (often treated as a 32-bit int internally for alignment, though it represents only 1 bit of information).

blocks.label: boolean Examples
lines: boolean distinction = score >= 90;   // false — 85 is not >= 90

items.html: ⚠️ Java vs C/C++: In Java, boolean is not interchangeable with integers. You cannot write if (1) or cast a boolean to int. true and false are the only valid values — period.
💡 Naming convention: Boolean variables and methods are typically named with the is, has, can, or should prefix — isActive, hasPermission, canEdit — making the intent immediately clear.

sections.title: Java Literals — Writing Values in Code

blocks.text: A literal is a fixed value written directly in the source code — the actual data itself, not a variable or expression. Java supports several forms of literals for different data types.
Integer Literals

blocks.label: Integer Literal Forms
lines: int rgb        = 0xFF_A5_00;  // orange color in hex

blocks.text: Floating-Point Literals

blocks.label: Floating-Point Literal Forms
lines: double d1 = 3.14;         // standard decimal — double by default
double nan    = Double.NaN;                // 0.0 / 0.0 — Not a Number

blocks.text: char, boolean, and String Literals

blocks.label: Other Literal Types
lines: // char literal — SINGLE quotes, exactly ONE character
// String literal — DOUBLE quotes (non-primitive, but very common)
// null literal — for any reference type

blocks.text: Non-primitive types are also called reference types because a variable of this type stores a reference (memory address) to where the object data lives on the heap — not the data itself. All non-primitive types ultimately extend java.lang.Object.

rows: Immutable sequence of characters. Most used type in Java.
Fixed-size, ordered collection of same-type elements.
Blueprint for objects — groups state (fields) and behaviour (methods).
Contract — defines methods a class must implement.

blocks.text: String is by far the most commonly used non-primitive type in Java. It represents an immutable sequence of Unicode characters. Once created, a String's value cannot be changed — any modification creates a new String object.

blocks.label: String Essentials
lines: // Two ways to create a String
String s1 = "Hello";                // String literal — stored in String Pool
String s2 = new String("Hello");    // new object on heap — NOT recommended
name = name.toUpperCase();   // reassign the reference to a new String
System.out.println(a == b);         // true  — same pool object
System.out.println(a == c);         // false — different heap objects

items.html: ⚠️ Always use .equals() to compare String content — not ==. The == operator compares references (memory addresses), not the actual characters. This is one of the most common beginner bugs in Java.

💡 String Pool: When you write String s = "Java", Java checks if "Java" already exists in the String Pool (a special area of the heap). If yes, the same object is reused — no new allocation. This is why String a = "Java"; String b = "Java"; gives a == b → true.

blocks.text: Wrapper classes are object representations of Java's 8 primitive types. They exist because many parts of Java (like collections, generics, reflection) require objects, not primitives. Every primitive type has exactly one corresponding wrapper class.
Autoboxing and Unboxing (Java 5+)

Autoboxing is the automatic conversion of a primitive to its wrapper class. Unboxing is the reverse — automatic conversion of a wrapper to its primitive. Java does this conversion automatically wherever needed.

blocks.label: Wrapper Classes & Autoboxing Demo
lines: for (int n : numbers) {   // each Integer is unboxed to int

items.html: ⚠️ Autoboxing performance: Autoboxing creates new objects on the heap. In performance-critical loops, avoid autoboxing millions of times — it adds GC pressure. Use primitive arrays instead of ArrayList<Integer> when performance matters.
⚠️ NullPointerException trap: If a wrapper variable is null and you try to unbox it, Java throws a NullPointerException. Example: Integer x = null; int y = x; → NullPointerException at runtime.

blocks.text: Type casting is the process of converting a value from one data type to another. Java supports two kinds of casting for primitive types — and they behave very differently.
1. Widening Casting (Implicit / Automatic)
Converting a smaller type to a larger type. Java does this automatically — no code needed, no data loss. The hierarchy: byte → short → int → long → float → double

blocks.label: Widening Casting
lines: // char to int — char's Unicode value is used

blocks.text: 2. Narrowing Casting (Explicit / Manual)
Converting a larger type to a smaller type. Must be done manually by writing the target type in parentheses. Data loss may occur — the extra bits are simply discarded.

blocks.label: Narrowing Casting
lines: int    i = (int) d;       // double → int: decimal truncated (not rounded)
// int to byte — overflow may occur
byte b      = (byte) bigInt;  // 130 is outside byte range (-128 to 127)
System.out.println(b);         // -126  ← data corruption due to overflow

rows: Yes if you forget the cast operator
No — but result may be unexpected

sections.title: How to Choose the Right Data Type

blocks.text: Choosing the right data type makes your code correct, efficient, and readable. Here is a practical decision guide for real-world Java development:

items.title: Whole Numbers → int by default
items.text: Use int for counters, ages, IDs, indices, loop variables. Switch to long only when values might exceed 2.1 billion — timestamps, file sizes, world-scale counts.

items.title: Decimal Numbers → double by default
items.text: Use double for prices, measurements, scientific values, percentages. Only use float if memory is critically constrained (GPU buffers, ML model weights).

items.title: Money / Exact Decimals → BigDecimal
items.text: Never use float or double for money — they cannot represent 0.1 exactly. Use java.math.BigDecimal for financial calculations requiring exact precision.

items.title: Single Character → char
items.text: Use char for individual characters, grade letters, menu options. For sequences of characters always use String.

items.title: True/False States → boolean
items.text: Use boolean for flags, conditions, enable/disable switches. Name it with is/has/can prefix: isActive, hasRole, canEdit.

items.title: Small Memory-Critical → byte/short
items.text: Use byte for raw binary data, file I/O buffers, image pixels, network packets. Use short only in legacy protocols or large arrays where each byte matters.

rows: Max ~150, always whole number — int is the default
8.1 billion exceeds int's max of 2.1 billion
Decimal needed; double is default for decimal math
Exact decimal required — float/double have rounding errors
Only two states — true or false
byte saves memory; int is simpler for arithmetic
Standard — int is default for indices
High precision needed; double provides ~15 digits

blocks.text: Practice This Code — Live Editor
These are the most frequently asked Java interview questions on data types — from beginner to intermediate level.

items.q: Q1. How many primitive data types does Java have? Name them all.
items.a: Java has exactly 8 primitive data types: byte (1 byte), short (2 bytes), int (4 bytes), long (8 bytes), float (4 bytes), double (8 bytes), char (2 bytes), and boolean (JVM-dependent, ~1 bit). Their sizes are fixed by the Java specification regardless of the underlying platform — a key part of Java's 'Write Once, Run Anywhere' guarantee.

items.q: Q2. What is the difference between int and Integer in Java?
items.a: 'int' is a primitive type — it stores the value directly in memory (stack), cannot be null, has no methods, and is faster. 'Integer' is a wrapper class (non-primitive, object) — it wraps int in an Object, can be null, has utility methods like Integer.parseInt(), Integer.MAX_VALUE, Integer.toBinaryString(). Java auto-converts between them via autoboxing (int → Integer) and unboxing (Integer → int).

items.q: Q3. What is the default value of each primitive data type?
items.a: Default values apply ONLY to instance (class-level) and static variables — NOT local variables. Defaults: byte=0, short=0, int=0, long=0L, float=0.0f, double=0.0d, char='\u0000' (null character), boolean=false. Local variables must be explicitly initialized before use — the compiler enforces this with a 'variable might not have been initialized' error.

items.q: Q4. What is the difference between float and double? Which should you prefer?
items.a: float is 32-bit (4 bytes) — single precision, accurate to ~7 decimal digits. Requires 'f' suffix: 3.14f. double is 64-bit (8 bytes) — double precision, accurate to ~15-16 decimal digits. Decimal literals like 3.14 are double by default. Always prefer double for general calculations. Use float only in memory-constrained scenarios (large float arrays, ML model weights, GPU computations).

items.q: Q5. Why is char 2 bytes in Java but only 1 byte in C/C++?
items.a: In C/C++, char is 1 byte because it uses ASCII encoding (only 128-256 characters). Java uses UTF-16 Unicode encoding, which requires 2 bytes (16 bits) to represent characters from across all the world's writing systems — over 65,000 code points in the Basic Multilingual Plane. This makes Java char fundamentally different: it can store any Unicode character, not just ASCII. This is why Java programs work correctly with Indian scripts, Chinese characters, emoji, and symbols worldwide.

items.q: Q6. Can boolean be cast to int in Java? Can you use if (1) in Java?
items.a: No on both counts. Java boolean is strictly not interchangeable with integer types — unlike C/C++ where 1 is true and 0 is false. In Java, you cannot write if (1) — it is a compile error. You cannot cast boolean to int or vice versa. The only valid boolean values are the literals 'true' and 'false'. This strictness prevents entire categories of bugs common in C code.

items.q: Q7. What happens when you assign 128 to a byte in Java?
items.a: byte range is -128 to 127. If you write byte b = 128; it is a compile error — 'incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from int to byte'. If you force it with narrowing cast: byte b = (byte) 128; — the value wraps around to -128 due to two's complement overflow. Binary of 128 is 10000000 — as a signed 8-bit value this is -128. This is called integer overflow and is a common source of bugs in low-level programming.

items.q: Q8. Why should you not use float or double for money calculations?
items.a: float and double use IEEE 754 binary floating-point, which cannot represent many decimal fractions exactly — including 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3. For example, 0.1 + 0.2 in Java equals 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3. In financial calculations this tiny error accumulates into significant wrong amounts over millions of transactions. Use java.math.BigDecimal for exact decimal arithmetic in banking, e-commerce, and any financial application.

blocks.text: Test your understanding of Java Data Types. Try to answer each question before revealing the answer.

items.q: 1. What is the output? int a = 5; int b = 2; System.out.println(a / b); System.out.println(a % b);
items.a: Output: 2, then 1. Integer division truncates — 5/2 = 2 (not 2.5). The modulo operator % gives the remainder — 5%2 = 1. To get 2.5, you would need to cast: (double) a / b or 5.0 / 2.

items.q: 2. Will this compile? long l = 3000000000; Explain.
items.a: No — compile error: 'integer number too large'. Integer literals are int by default. 3000000000 (3 billion) exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE (2,147,483,647). The compiler rejects it before even considering the long target type. Fix: long l = 3_000_000_000L; — add the L suffix to tell the compiler it is a long literal.

items.q: 3. What is the output? char c = 'A'; System.out.println(c + 1); System.out.println((char)(c + 1));
items.a: Line 1: 66 (int). When you do arithmetic on char, Java promotes it to int and returns int — 'A' is 65, 65+1=66. Line 2: B. By casting (char)(66) back to char, you get the character at Unicode point 66, which is 'B'.

items.q: 4. What data type would you use to store a 12-digit Aadhaar number? Why?
items.a: long. A 12-digit number like 234567890123 is approximately 2.3 × 10^11. This exceeds int's max of ~2.1 × 10^9 (2,147,483,647). long handles up to 9.2 × 10^18, so it fits easily. Note: in practice, you might store it as a String to preserve leading zeros and because you don't do arithmetic on ID numbers.

items.q: 5. What is the output and why? double d = 0.1 + 0.2; System.out.println(d); System.out.println(d == 0.3);
items.a: Output: 0.30000000000000004, then false. IEEE 754 binary floating-point cannot represent 0.1 or 0.2 exactly — they are infinite repeating binary fractions. Adding them gives 0.30000000000000004, not exactly 0.3. Therefore d == 0.3 is false. This is why you should never compare floating-point values with == — use Math.abs(d - 0.3) < 1e-10 instead. For exact arithmetic, use BigDecimal.

items.q: 6. What is the difference between String s1 = 'Java' and String s2 = new String('Java')? Which is better?
items.a: s1 = "Java" creates a String in the String Pool (or reuses an existing one). If another variable also points to "Java", they share the same object. s2 = new String("Java") always creates a new String object on the heap, separate from the pool. s1 == s1 is true (same pool object), but s1 == s2 is false (different objects). String literals (s1 style) are preferred — they save memory through pool reuse and are more readable.

items.q: 7. What is the result of (byte)(200)? Explain the calculation.
items.a: Result: -56. 200 in binary (8 bits) is 11001000. As a signed 8-bit two's complement value: the leftmost bit (1) means negative. To find the value: flip all bits (00110111 = 55) and add 1 = 56, then negate = -56. Alternatively: 200 - 256 = -56 (since byte wraps at 256). This demonstrates overflow in narrowing casting.

items.q: 8. Can you store the value 65535 in a char? Can you store -1 in a char?
items.a: 65535: Yes. char is an unsigned 16-bit integer with range 0 to 65535. char c = (char) 65535; is valid — it represents \uFFFF (a special Unicode character). -1: No directly. char cannot hold negative values — it is unsigned. However, (char)(-1) in Java results in 65535 (\uFFFF) due to binary representation, since -1 in two's complement 16-bit is all 1s = 65535. So the cast works but gives 65535, not -1.

items.a: Wrapper classes are object representations of the 8 primitive types: Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Float, Double, Character, Boolean. They are needed when an object is required (collections like ArrayList only hold objects, not primitives). Java automatically converts between primitives and wrappers via autoboxing (primitive to wrapper) and unboxing (wrapper to primitive).
